A count of animals mixes the number present with the chance of
detecting each one. A single survey cannot tell a large population
counted poorly from a small one counted well. N-mixture models
separate the two with replicate visits made while the population is
closed to change (Royle
[2004](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0006-341X.2004.00142.x)). The mean
of the replicate counts reflects abundance times detection. Their
spread reflects detection alone.

The `nmix()` family places this model inside an mvgam state-space
model. The latent abundance can then follow a temporal trend, respond
to covariates through `trend_formula` and be forecast. This article
simulates yearly surveys of four species whose abundances respond to
temperature in different ways, while wind lowers the chance of
detecting them. One model recovers each species' abundance in every
year, the two covariate effects and a forecast of the counts.

## The model

Species $s$ is counted on visit $r$ in year $t$. Each count is a
binomial draw from the $N_{s,t}$ individuals present:

\begin{align*}
y_{s,t,r} & \sim \text{Binomial}(N_{s,t}, p_{s,t,r}) \\
N_{s,t} & \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_{s,t}) \\
\log \lambda_{s,t} & = \alpha_s + f_s(\text{temp}_t) + z_{s,t} \\
z_{s,t} & \sim \text{Normal}(\phi_s z_{s,t-1}, \sigma_s) \\
\text{logit}(p_{s,t,r}) & = \gamma_s + \delta \, \text{wind}_{s,t,r}
\end{align*}

Each species has its own smooth response $f_s$ to temperature. Its
AR(1) state $z_s$ absorbs the year-to-year change that temperature
leaves unexplained. Each species also has its own detection intercept
$\gamma_s$. All species share one wind effect $\delta$ on detection.

Because Hamiltonian Monte Carlo cannot sample the integer $N_{s,t}$,
mvgam sums the likelihood over every value of $N$ from the largest
count up to a cap. Stan then samples only continuous parameters. The
Stan User's Guide chapter on
[latent discrete parameters](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/latent-discrete.html)
describes the technique.

## The data

To compare estimates with known abundances, we simulate four species
surveyed on five visits in each of 20 years. The first species'
abundance rises with temperature and levels off. The second peaks at
intermediate temperatures. The third declines. The fourth has a weak
U shape. On every visit, the detection probability falls with wind
speed.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(11)
n_sp <- 4
n_year <- 20
n_visit <- 5
species <- paste0("sp_", seq_len(n_sp))

# A yearly temperature index with mean 0 and SD 1
temp <- round(as.numeric(scale(
  cumsum(rnorm(n_year, 0, 0.6)) + rnorm(n_year)
)), 2)

# AR(1) deviations in log abundance that temperature leaves unexplained
z <- matrix(0, n_year, n_sp)
for (t in 2:n_year) z[t, ] <- 0.6 * z[t - 1, ] + rnorm(n_sp, 0, 0.2)

# Each species' response to temperature on the log scale: a
# saturating rise, a hump, a decline and a weak U
temp_effect <- cbind(
  0.8 * tanh(1.5 * temp),
  0.6 - 0.6 * temp^2,
  -0.5 * temp,
  0.2 * temp^2 - 0.2
)

# Abundance N each year, around baselines of 30, 12, 20 and 10
log_lambda <- sweep(temp_effect + z, 2, log(c(30, 12, 20, 10)), "+")
N <- matrix(rpois(n_year * n_sp, exp(log_lambda)), n_year, n_sp)

# Logit detection intercept of each species
det_sp <- rnorm(n_sp, 0.3, 0.4)

# One row per visit, with wind speed recorded on each
dat <- expand.grid(visit = seq_len(n_visit), time = seq_len(n_year),
                   series = factor(species, levels = species))
dat$temp <- temp[dat$time]
dat$wind <- round(runif(nrow(dat)), 2)
dat$N <- N[cbind(dat$time, as.integer(dat$series))]

# Each individual present is counted with probability p, which falls
# with wind speed
p <- plogis(det_sp[dat$series] - 1.5 * dat$wind)
dat$y <- rbinom(nrow(dat), dat$N, p)

# Upper bound of the sum over N in each closure unit
dat$cap <- 80L
head(dat)
```

Each row is one visit. `series` names the species and `time` the
year. The visits that share a `(series, time)` pair form one closure
unit, over which $N$ is fixed. `cap` bounds the sum over $N$ in each
unit. It must be at least the unit's largest count. The model cannot
estimate an abundance above it. The simulated abundances peak at
`r max(dat$N)`, which leaves room below a cap of 80. Each unit of cap
adds a term to the sum in every closure unit at every iteration. The
`N` column holds the simulated abundance for comparison. The model
never sees it.

The last three years are held out to score a forecast:

```{r split}
train <- subset(dat, time <= 17)
test <- subset(dat, time > 17)
```

## Fitting the model

To estimate abundance and detection together, we put one formula on
each inside `bf()`. The first describes abundance. The second, `p ~`,
describes detection. `trend_formula` describes the latent
log-abundance. In it, `by = lv_axis()` gives each species its own
smooth of temperature. `AR()` gives each species its own AR(1) state:

```{r fit}
mod <- mvgam(
  bf(y ~ series, p ~ series + wind),
  trend_formula = ~ s(temp, by = lv_axis(), k = 5) + AR(),
  data = train,
  newdata = test,
  family = nmix(),
  chains = 4, seed = 11, silent = 2
)
```

```{r summary}
summary(mod)
```

```{r wind-numbers, include = FALSE}
wind <- as.numeric(as_draws_matrix(mod, variable = "b_p_wind"))
fe_wind <- sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", mean(wind),
                   quantile(wind, 0.025), quantile(wind, 0.975))
```

The wind coefficient `p_wind` is `r fe_wind` on the logit scale,
against the simulated value of $-1.5$.

## Latent abundance

`hindcast(type = "latent_state")` returns the posterior of $N$ in each
closure unit, conditional on the counts observed there. Its `plot()`
method returns a `ggplot`, to which we add the simulated abundances
and the largest count of each year:

```{r latent-plot, fig.asp = 0.75, fig.cap = "Posterior medians with 50% and 95% credible intervals of each species' abundance. Black points are the simulated abundances. Open circles are the largest count in each year."}
hc <- hindcast(mod, type = "latent_state")
truth <- unique(train[, c("series", "time", "N")])
counts <- aggregate(y ~ series + time, data = train, FUN = max)
plot(hc) +
  geom_point(data = counts, aes(x = time, y = y), shape = 21,
             fill = "white", colour = "grey30", size = 1.6) +
  geom_point(data = truth, aes(x = time, y = N), size = 1.6)
```

```{r coverage, include = FALSE}
state <- merge(as.data.frame(hc), truth, by = c("series", "time"))
state <- merge(state, counts, by = c("series", "time"))
n_covered <- sum(state$N >= state$lower_95 & state$N <= state$upper_95)
n_above <- sum(state$median > state$y)
```

Because detection is imperfect, every count falls below the abundance
it came from. The posterior median of $N$ exceeds the largest count in
`r n_above` of the `r nrow(state)` species-years. Its 95% intervals
contain the simulated abundance in `r n_covered` of them. A model of
the counts alone would report every population as smaller than it is.

## Covariate effects

`conditional_effects()` accepts the N-mixture prediction types. With
`type = "latent_state"` it draws the expected abundance against
temperature. `series = "all"` gives each species its own panel:

```{r temp-effects, fig.asp = 0.75, fig.cap = "Expected abundance of each species against temperature, with 95% credible intervals."}
plot(
  conditional_effects(mod, effects = "temp", type = "latent_state",
                      series = "all"),
  ask = FALSE
)
```

The four smooths take the shapes we simulated: a saturating rise, a
hump, a decline and a shallow U. With `type = "detection"`,
`conditional_effects()` draws the detection probability against wind
speed:

```{r wind-effect, out.width = "70%", fig.cap = "Detection probability against wind speed, with its 95% credible interval."}
plot(conditional_effects(mod, effects = "wind", type = "detection"),
     ask = FALSE)
```

## Forecasts

`forecast()` advances each species' AR(1) state through the held-out
years. It combines the state with the temperature smooths and passes
the result through detection. The forecast is of the count on each
held-out visit:

```{r forecast, fig.asp = 0.75, fig.cap = "Counts predicted on each visit over the training years and the three held-out years. Points are the observed counts."}
fc <- forecast(mod)
plot(fc)
```

`score()` evaluates the forecast against the held-out counts. The
[forecast evaluation article](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/forecast_evaluation.html)
compares models on such scores.

## Checking the fit

To test whether the model reproduces the variation among visits,
`pp_check(type = "fit_stat")` sums the counts of each closure unit. It
measures their discrepancy from the expected sum with the chi-squared
statistic of MacKenzie and Bailey
([2004](https://doi.org/10.1198/108571104X3361)). It repeats the
calculation on counts replicated from the posterior:

```{r fit-stat}
fit_stat <- pp_check(mod, type = "fit_stat")
fit_stat
```

```{r fit-stat-numbers, include = FALSE}
fe_fit <- if (fit_stat$bayes_p > 0.05) {
  "gives no sign of lack of fit"
} else {
  "suggests the model misses some variation among visits"
}
```

A Bayesian p-value near 0 would mean the replicates rarely reach the
discrepancy of the observed counts. The value here,
`r sprintf("%.2f", fit_stat$bayes_p)`, `r fe_fit`.
`latent_N_saturation()` reports the posterior probability that $N$
reaches the cap in each unit:

```{r saturation}
sat <- latent_N_saturation(mod)
max(sat$p_saturated)
```

The largest probability any unit gives to reaching the cap of 80 is
`r sprintf("%.3f", max(sat$p_saturated))`.

## Other observation processes

The binomial observation process assumes each individual present is
detected independently on each visit. `nmix()` offers two more through
its `type` argument. All three marginalise the latent abundance in the
same way. Every method used above works with each of them.

| Variant | Constructor | Response | Detection |
|---------|-------------|----------|-----------|
| Poisson-binomial (Royle 2004) | `nmix()` | Counts that cannot exceed $N$ | Probability $p$ per individual and visit, logit link |
| Royle-Nichols (Royle and Nichols 2003) | `nmix("royle_nichols")` | Detection or non-detection | Probability $r$ per individual. A visit detects the species with probability $1 - (1 - r)^N$ |
| Poisson-Poisson | `nmix("poisson_poisson")` | Counts that can record one individual more than once | Encounter rate $p$ per individual and visit, log link |

## Summary

From five counts a year, the N-mixture model recovered abundances that
the counts alone understate. Its 95% intervals covered the simulated
abundance in `r n_covered` of `r nrow(state)` species-years. The same
fit recovered four differently shaped responses to temperature and the
wind effect on detection. Because the abundance follows an mvgam
trend, the fit also forecast the held-out counts. All of this came
from one `mvgam()` call with `family = nmix()`, whose observation
formula describes detection while its trend formula describes the
latent abundance.

## Where to next

Each function used here has a help page, such as `?nmix` or
`?latent_N_saturation`, with its arguments and output. `?nmix` gives the identification conditions and default
priors of each variant. `pivot_detection_array()` converts detection
arrays from unmarked, spOccupancy or ubms into the long format used
here. `occ()` fits occupancy models to the same layout.
`how_to_cite()` writes a methods paragraph for a fitted model, citing
the N-mixture variant it used. `methods_md()` writes out its
equations.

Related articles:

- [Joint species distribution models](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/jsdgam.html)
  share latent factors among many species.
- [Integrated distribution models](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/idm.html)
  combine several survey protocols that observe one population.
- [Formatting data for mvgam](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/data.html)
  covers the checks `mvgam_data()` runs on closure-unit data.
